Any pilot, or any scientist or engineer Level 1 or higher can use their EVA chute when they have one in their inventory.  It can be deployed and repackaged, just like vessel chutes.

These chutes are vastly more advanced through the use of ram air cells and control handles to allow the kerbal to adjust their glide angle like a plane!
Kerbals with sufficient experience can now enjoy the feeling of flight (without crashing at the end) by using their EVA chute.
Here you will find out about CommNet and KerbNet functionality.

Communication Networks allow your vessels to transmit data between each other and Kerbin. You can 
create a CommNet with antennas which connect back to Kerbin’s Deep Space Network (DSN).

These links are used for Control and for Science. You can extend the range and Signal Strength of DSN 
connections by upgrading the Tracking Station and can increase coverage and Signal Strength further 
with Relays.

A control link is a connection from the vessel back to a control source. This control source is either a 
Pilot Kerbal in a vessel that offers remote control, or any of the ground stations on Kerbin (which are 
presumably staffed by ace pilots). A vessel which requires but lacks a control source will suffer reduced 
control abilities.
Any vessel which lacks a Pilot Kerbal requires a control source for full control. Other kerbals can add \nsome control ability but cannot provide full control.

The current control path, as well as all potential links, and the whole network can be visualized in map \nview and the tracking station. A panel shows relevant CommNet information including control level, \nsignal strength, and destination type.

The maximum range at which two antennas can communicate is the square root of the product of their 
powers (the geometric mean). Antenna powers are divided into six classes, Class 0 through Class 5. 

Class 0 antennas are the internal antennas on pod and probe cores; the other classes are standalone 
parts. The DSN also has three power levels, one for each Tracking Station level.

Most antennas can combine their power with each other on the same vessel. However, doing so has 
diminishing returns.

Sometimes, you are unable to get to a control point either due to extreme range, or because \nsomething is in the way (terrain, or another orbital body).  Relay antennas allow a signal to be \n‘bounced’ from a vessel, to a relay, then onto a control point or even another relay!
Or boost signal strength by \nhaving a low power antenna \ntransmit via a high power relay.
